prize_parts.citation: For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of one DNA base into another without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from halide perovskites (B047) to base editing (B007) for Liu, Komor and Gaudelli. Round 1 showed that the perovskite case fails on exactly the two tests I would apply to any candidate: a three-name credit cut that cannot be defended (Miyasaka, Snaith and Park against Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis), and a practical consequence that is not yet demonstrated outside the laboratory because stability and lead content remain open. Base editing passes both better. It is a defined molecular design: an evolved deaminase tethered to a nickase or impaired Cas protein performs a specific chemical conversion on one nucleotide, with the mechanism stated and the editor classes separable. The cytosine editor (Komor, Liu) and the adenine editor (Gaudelli, Liu), the latter requiring directed evolution of TadA because no natural DNA adenine deaminase exists, are two clearly attributable inventions. The claim has been replicated by many independent laboratories, a large derivative toolbox exists, and clinical benefit is being reported. It is a method that lets a whole community do what it could not do before, which is the kind of enabling achievement I value most. It was my own third choice and the broadest first-place base on the shortlist, but I rest the move on the evidence and not on the count.
statement.case_against: The 2020 prize recognised CRISPR-Cas9, and some members will read base editing as a successor within one genome-editing story. I do not agree, since the chemistry is different (deamination and mismatch-repair logic, not double-strand cleavage), but I understand the objection. Attribution is not clean: Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID work was independent and near-contemporaneous, and under a three-name limit a Liu-centred trio leaves them out and gives two seats to Liu's former trainees. Long-term safety, bystander edits and off-target deamination are still being characterised, so the clinical record is not yet long. I also give up the materials and energy chemistry I know best, and I accept that a prize built on halide perovskites may be right in a later year once stability and credit are better settled.

responses.point: Proposes Liu, Komor and Gaudelli for base editing, as a defined enzymatic chemistry whose founding inventions are separable, while naming CRISPR proximity and Target-AID as reservations.
responses.response: I now share your configuration and I agree with the core of your reasoning: deamination under programmable control without a double-strand break is a distinct chemical mechanism, and the cytosine and adenine editors are two separable inventions. My structural-chemist test is whether the claimed mechanism was actually established. Here it was: the nickase-directed strand choice, the uracil glycosylase inhibitor and the evolved TadA are experimentally dissected, not asserted. I part from you only on tone about Target-AID. Kondo and Nishida cannot be dismissed as a footnote, and the citation should be worded around the two editor classes so that it describes what Liu, Komor and Gaudelli did and does not claim to cover all priority.

responses.point: Proposes a two-part prize pairing Buchwald and Hartwig for Pd-catalysed C-N coupling with base editing for Liu alone, conceding thin opening support for B065 and no unifying theme.
responses.response: In round 1 I said I would keep perovskites behind base editing and C-N coupling, and I still respect the maturity of Buchwald-Hartwig chemistry. I do not support the pairing, for two reasons you largely concede yourself. First, a prize joining synthesis methodology and genome engineering has no shared theme to explain to a general audience. Second, a Liu-only base editing part is the weaker attribution: it removes Komor and Gaudelli, who are the first inventors of the two editor classes, and it does not remove the Target-AID question. If the committee wants one prize that honours the editors, I prefer three names in a single part, and I would judge C-N coupling on its own merits against the 2010 palladium prize and the earlier Kosugi work.

responses.point: As chair, proposes base editing for Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as the configuration he can best defend to a general audience, and had ranked perovskites eighth for maturity.
responses.response: I accept your maturity argument and I moved partly because of it: stability and lead toxicity are the open facts on perovskites, and I argued in round 1 that this should not hold back a discovery prize. On reflection the credit problem is the stronger objection and it is separate from timing. I agree with your answer to the chair's question on CRISPR: the 2020 prize recognised cleavage-based editing and the base editors are a different chemical invention. Your framing of Komor and Gaudelli as inventors of the two editor classes is the most defensible way to fill the three seats. I would still ask that the committee state plainly why Kondo and Nishida are not named, because a silent omission would be criticised.

responses.point: Proposes Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli for targeted protein degradation by bifunctional molecules, and states that this leaves out the cereblon and molecular-glue work of Handa and Ito.
responses.response: I took your question to me seriously. I think a single induced-proximity citation that includes both PROTACs and glues would need Crews or Deshaies, Ciulli and either Handa or Gray, and I cannot identify one three-name cut that does not leave out someone whose mechanistic contribution is decisive. The ternary-complex structures and the cereblon identification are strong structural evidence, which is why B011 remains my first alternative. But a citation naming only bifunctional PROTACs would misdescribe the field, as you say, and the absence of an approved degrader still counts against it this year. I would be comfortable moving to B011 if the committee settles on a definition and, ideally, a first approval.

responses.point: Proposes B011 for Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, weighting the breadth of support across all eight opening ballots, and applies a consequence test, calling perovskites premature.
responses.response: You applied a consequence test to my perovskite proposal and I have conceded it. I would apply the same test to B011, and the missing approval, which you say you cannot confirm, is the open item. Base editing has already given patient-level clinical reports, so on your own criterion it is closer to ready. I do not rely on breadth of ranking as merit, and you say you do not either; the difference between us is whether three-name credit is defensible. I find Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli defensible for PROTACs but not as a description of the whole degradation field, whereas Liu, Komor and Gaudelli describe base editing cleanly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts base editing as distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize or holds it for a longer clinical record
Whether Kondo and Nishida should displace Komor or Gaudelli within the three-name limit
Whether PROTACs and molecular glues can be defined as one achievement with a defensible three-name credit, and whether a first degrader approval is imminent
Whether halide perovskites would be better judged in a later year once stability and credit are clearer
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I remain a Stockholm University colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski, who proposes B028; I regard this as collegial and not a recusal matter. My own field overlaps B047 only through general materials chemistry and none of the candidates is a collaborator.
